prompt: What does a cloud security posture management tool read?
hint: Posture is a state, read through the API.

choices.text: The versions of the libraries an application depends on
choices.why: That is a vulnerability scanner's job, which lesson 13 runs over a function's dependencies.

choices.text: The account's configuration, compared with rules
choices.why: Right: which buckets are public, which ports are open, who has MFA, read again and again.

choices.text: The events of who did what, as they happen, to raise alerts
choices.why: That is threat detection, such as GuardDuty. It reacts to actions; CSPM reads settings.

choices.text: The provider's own data centres, through its compliance reports
choices.why: Those are the provider's half and are read once, as documents. CSPM reads the customer's half, through the API.

prompt: A consultant audited the clinic's account in March and found it clean. Why does the lesson say that report says little about October?
hint: Lesson 1's request printed nothing.

choices.text: Because consultants check fewer rules than a CSPM product
choices.why: Maybe, maybe not; the point holds even for a perfect audit.

choices.text: Any change since March was one quiet API call away
choices.why: Right. Posture is a reading, not a certificate, and it goes stale at the speed of the API.

choices.text: Because AWS resets the configuration of every account each quarter
choices.why: AWS changes nothing in your configuration; people with keys do.

choices.text: Audit reports expire legally after six months
choices.why: No such rule is involved. The problem is technical: the state moves.

prompt: Match each kind of tool to what it reads.
hint: Three neighbours, three different jobs.

prompt: Last night a key was used to read every patient export. This morning's CSPM scan is clean. What does the clean scan tell you about the night?
hint: What does CSPM read, and what does it not?

choices.text: That the reading was authorised, since a clean scan means the account is configured as intended
choices.why: A correct configuration can still be used by somebody holding a stolen key.

choices.text: Nothing: CSPM reads settings, and the night is in the event records
choices.why: Right. It finds the open door and cannot say whether somebody walked through; lesson 15's records can.

choices.text: That the key has already been revoked
choices.why: Nothing in a scan revokes anything, and a scanner of four rules never looked at that key.

choices.text: That the exports were encrypted, so nothing could be read
choices.why: Encryption at rest does not stop a principal with permission to read; lesson 11.

prompt: Of the four faults placed in the account, which one is not a mistake?
hint: A website is meant to be read by strangers.

choices.text: SSH open to the world on `booking-admin`
choices.why: That one is a mistake: lesson 8 gives caio a way in that is not the whole internet.

choices.text: bia's user without a second factor
choices.why: A person signing in with one factor is lesson 6's fault, and it is fixed.

choices.text: The public policy on `clinic-web`
choices.why: Right. It holds the public website, so it gets an exception rather than a fix.

choices.text: The missing default encryption on `clinic-exports`, which holds patient exports
choices.why: Patient exports are the last thing to leave unencrypted; it is fixed.

prompt: moto registered caio's MFA device with the codes `123456` and `654321`. What would AWS have done with the same call?
hint: The two codes have to come from the device.

choices.text: Refused it: the codes must match the device's secret
choices.why: Right. Not run here: moto records the device without checking.

choices.text: Accepted it, because any six digits are a valid code
choices.why: A code is valid only if the device's secret produces it at that moment.

choices.text: Accepted it and sent caio an e-mail to confirm
choices.why: There is no e-mail step; the two consecutive codes are the confirmation.

prompt: `scan.py` never writes an endpoint address. How does it reach moto rather than AWS?
hint: The same file every lesson reads.

choices.text: boto3 reads `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` and the rest from the variables `env.sh` sets
choices.why: Right: the same variables that point the command line at moto point the library at it.

choices.text: boto3 finds moto by scanning the ports of the local machine until one answers like AWS
choices.why: It does nothing of the kind; it goes where its configuration says.

choices.text: It talks to the AWS command line, which forwards each request
choices.why: boto3 sends its own requests; the command line is not involved.

choices.text: moto installs a patched copy of boto3 that already knows which port moto listens on
choices.why: boto3 is the ordinary library; the environment does the pointing.

prompt: Which of these would `scan.py`, as written, miss? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the list of what the fifty-six lines leave out.

choices.text: A security group in `us-east-1` with port 22 open to the world
choices.why: Right. It reads one region, the one `env.sh` names.

choices.text: An object made public by an ACL
choices.why: Right. The bucket rule reads policies and not ACLs.

choices.text: A bucket in `sa-east-1` with no default encryption
choices.why: That is one of its four rules, and it found `clinic-exports`.

choices.text: A user of the account with no MFA device
choices.why: Found: bia was listed.

choices.text: When the bucket became public
choices.why: Right. It remembers nothing between runs; AWS Config records history.

prompt: Why does `scan.py` end with `sys.exit(1 if still_open else 0)`?
hint: Who reads an exit code?

choices.text: So that a pipeline stops on an open finding without reading the text
choices.why: Right. Lesson 14 uses exactly that to make a gate.

choices.text: Python needs an explicit exit or the output is lost
choices.why: Output is printed as it goes; the exit code is extra information.

choices.text: Because moto refuses the next connection from any program that exited with 0 before
choices.why: moto never sees the exit code.

choices.text: To delete the findings once they are printed
choices.why: An exit code deletes nothing.

prompt: A security group has one rule: every protocol (`-1`), from `0.0.0.0/0`, with no port numbers. Does `scan.py` report it?
hint: What do the missing `FromPort` and `ToPort` default to?

choices.text: No, since the rule names no port at all
choices.why: A rule with no ports covers every port, which is worse, and the defaults treat it so.

choices.text: Yes, twice: once for port 22 and once for 3389
choices.why: Right. The defaults 0 and 65535 make the range cover both ports.

choices.text: Yes, once, for the protocol rather than for a port
choices.why: It loops over the two ports and appends a finding for each one the range covers.

choices.text: It crashes, because `FromPort` is missing
choices.why: `rule.get("FromPort", 0)` supplies a default instead of failing.

prompt: What does the lesson say an exception must carry?
hint: Two things besides the rule and the resource.

choices.text: The approval of the cloud provider
choices.why: The provider has no say in your exceptions.

choices.text: A reason and an end date
choices.why: Right. Without the date it is permanent and nobody remembers why.

choices.text: A screenshot proving the resource is safe today
choices.why: Today's state is what the scanner reads; an exception records a decision about it.

choices.text: The number of findings it hides
choices.why: An exception covers one rule on one resource.

prompt: The exception for `clinic-web` ends on 2027-04-30. On 2027-05-02 nobody has touched it. What does `scan.py` print for that bucket?
hint: Compare `until` with today.

choices.text: `accepted`, because the line is still in `accepted.txt`
choices.why: The line is there, and its date has passed, so it no longer covers the finding.

choices.text: Nothing: an expired exception removes the bucket from the scan
choices.why: The bucket is always read; the exception only decides how the finding is shown.

choices.text: `OPEN`, and the exit code is 1
choices.why: Right. An expired exception reopens the finding without anybody remembering to.

choices.text: An error, because the date is in the past
choices.why: A past date parses perfectly; it just fails the comparison.

prompt: Put the steps of the lesson's posture loop in order, from the first scan to catching drift.
hint: Proof comes after every fix.
items: scan and get four open findings
write a dated exception for the website
scan again and get none open
trap: Putting the exception after the second scan is the slip: it has to exist before the scan that is meant to come back clean.

prompt: caio opened port 22 to the world after the clean scan, and nothing stopped him. Why not?
hint: A scan reads; it does not guard.

choices.text: A scanner only reads; he is allowed to change his own group
choices.why: Right. That is drift, and catching it is the next scan's job.

choices.text: The exception for `clinic-web` also covered security groups
choices.why: It covers one rule on one bucket.

choices.text: moto does not enforce security groups
choices.why: Enforcement of traffic is beside the point: the change itself was allowed, and would be on AWS too.

choices.text: Scans stop running after one comes back clean
choices.why: The point of the loop is that they do not stop.

prompt: Which of these shrink drift rather than only catching it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two things, from lessons 12 and 14.

choices.text: Writing the configuration as code, so the next apply undoes a hand change
choices.why: Right, lesson 12.

choices.text: Running the check in the deployment flow, before the change reaches the account
choices.why: Right, lesson 14.

choices.text: Scanning once a quarter instead of every morning
choices.why: That catches less drift, later.

choices.text: Adding an exception for every open finding
choices.why: That hides drift; it does not shrink it.

prompt: When the configuration moves away from the state that was checked, through a change made after the check, that is called ___.
hint: One word, from the section's last heading.

prompt: Which AWS service records every change to a resource's configuration, so it can say when a bucket became public?
hint: The inventory with a memory.

choices.text: GuardDuty
choices.why: GuardDuty reads events for threats; it keeps no configuration history.

choices.text: AWS Config
choices.why: Right. Config rules then judge each recorded change.

choices.text: AWS Organizations
choices.why: Organizations groups accounts; it records no configuration.

choices.text: IAM Access Analyzer
choices.why: It reasons about access policies, not about the history of every resource.

prompt: Match each tool to where it comes from.
hint: Three providers and an open-source project.

prompt: What permissions does the lesson say a scanner such as Prowler should run with?
hint: A tool that looks for exposure must not become one.

choices.text: `AdministratorAccess`, since a scanner has to read every service and every setting in it
choices.why: Reading every service does not need the right to change any of them.

choices.text: A role that reads everything and changes nothing, such as `SecurityAudit`
choices.why: Right. More than that turns the scanner into an exposure of its own.

choices.text: The root user's key, so that no service, region or setting is hidden from it
choices.why: The root user should have no key at all, and certainly not one handed to a tool.

choices.text: No credentials, since it reads only public information
choices.why: Configuration is not public; the scanner has to authenticate.

prompt: The clinic has one account and four people. According to the lesson, when does a provider's posture service earn its price?
hint: Three situations are named.

choices.text: From day one, because auditors refuse to take a home-made scanner as evidence of the account's posture
choices.why: The lesson says the four rules running every morning are enough to start with.

choices.text: Never, since its rules are the same as `scan.py`'s
choices.why: It carries hundreds of rules, every region and history; `scan.py` has four rules in one region.

choices.text: When accounts multiply, an auditor asks for history, or nobody has time to maintain the rules
choices.why: Right, the three the lesson names.

choices.text: Only once the account has been breached and the team needs a tool to show what went wrong
choices.why: Posture management exists to find the open door before anybody walks through it.

prompt: In the first scan, how many findings were open?
hint: One per fault placed.

prompt: After the fixes and the exception, caio reopened port 22. How many findings did the last scan report as open?
hint: The website stays accepted.

prompt: The CIS ___ are the published rule lists most posture tools start from.
hint: From the Center for Internet Security.

prompt: A CSPM product reports 900 findings on its first run, and the team decides to accept all of them for a year so the dashboard turns green. What has the team actually done?
hint: What is an exception for?

choices.text: Fixed the posture, since accepted findings no longer count
choices.why: Nothing in the account changed; only the report did.

choices.text: Turned the list into noise: exceptions nobody weighed are fixes nobody made
choices.why: Right. Exceptions are decisions, one at a time, with a reason somebody could disagree with.

choices.text: Followed the lesson exactly, since each of the 900 exceptions carries an end date a year away
choices.why: The date is half of it; the reason, weighed per finding, is the other half.

choices.text: Nothing harmful, because the product will reopen the whole lot by itself when next year comes
choices.why: For a year every real fault is hidden among the accepted ones.
